# Curves

- Route: `/tools/photo-curves`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `photo-curves`

## Summary

Shape tone and color with a draggable curve for RGB and each channel, through up to 16 points, with an eyedropper. (Photo editing)

## Details

Curves maps every input tone to an output tone along a line you draw, and it is the most flexible tonal and color tool in any editor. Aperture gives you four curves, RGB, Red, Green and Blue, each with 2 to 16 draggable points, and a Pick a point eyedropper that adds a point at the value under the cursor in the photo. The curve through the points is a monotone cubic, so it never overshoots or reverses between points, and it is sampled into a 256-entry table that the GPU and the export server both read with linear interpolation. The three color curves are applied first and the RGB curve last, in the gamma-space tonal stage of the layer stack, under a live histogram and with the usual mask, opacity and blend mode controls on the layer.
### What it does
- Adds a Curves layer with four graphs, RGB, Red, Green and Blue; drag points on the graph, add up to 16 per curve and remove any point except the ends.
- Fits a monotone cubic Hermite curve through the points so an S-curve stays smooth and a steep step never produces a reversal.
- Samples each curve into 256 entries and applies the color curves first, then the RGB curve to the result.
- Picks points from the photo with an eyedropper so a specific skin tone or sky value becomes a handle on the graph.
- Shows the result on the live histogram and exports it from the original at full resolution.
### How to use it
1. Drop a photo: The editor opens with the Curves panel and the RGB graph in front.
2. Place points: Click the graph or use the eyedropper on the photo to add points, then drag them to shape the curve.
3. Work the channels: Switch to Red, Green or Blue to correct a cast or to add a color grade with opposing curves.
4. Export: Choose a format and size; the server builds the same tables and renders the original.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Each curve becomes a 256-entry table; steep curves on 8-bit sources can expose gaps in the histogram, so export PNG when that matters.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- Points must have strictly increasing x from 0 to 1. The slopes at the points use the Fritsch-Carlson method: secant slopes d between neighbors, an end slope equal to the first or last secant, inner slopes equal to the average of the two secants (or 0 where the secants change sign), and any pair of slopes whose squared ratio to the secant exceeds 9 is scaled back so the segment cannot overshoot.
- Each curve is sampled at 256 values of x = i / 255 using the cubic Hermite basis (2t cubed - 3t squared + 1, t cubed - 2t squared + t, and their complements) and clamped to 0..1; x values before the first point take its y and x values after the last point take its y. A pixel value is then read from the table by linear interpolation between the two nearest entries, which is what the GPU's linear sampler does.
- A symmetric S-curve through (0.25, 0.2) and (0.75, 0.8) turns 0.4 into 0.3716, 0.6 into 0.6284 and leaves 0.5 at exactly 0.5; its table entries 127 and 128 are 0.4975 and 0.5025, and sampling 0.5 lands halfway between them.
- Order inside the layer: Red, Green and Blue curves map their own channel, then the RGB curve maps all three results. Because the fit is monotone, a steep three-point step from (0.4, 0.1) to (0.5, 0.9) peaks at exactly 1 with no ringing, where a plain cubic spline would overshoot above 1 and below 0 next to the step.
- The preview you drag the curve against is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same tables and interpolation, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance of a few 8-bit levels at most (grain is exact).
### When not to use it
Curves is overkill when all the photo needs is a black and white point, which the Levels panel sets with two sliders and a histogram, or when a single global contrast or brightness change will do, which the Basic panel handles in one move. Exposure problems belong in the Exposure sliders, since they work in linear light and curves do not. And if a grade already exists as a .cube file, the LUT page applies the exact table rather than a hand-drawn approximation of it.
### Use cases
- Gentle S-curve for punch: Points at (0.25, 0.2) and (0.75, 0.8) on RGB: shadows down about 13 levels at 0.25, highlights up the same at 0.75, mid-gray untouched.
- Matte fade: Raise the first RGB point to y = 0.08 so pure black becomes 20 of 255, and add (0.3, 0.3) to keep the midtones in place.
- Cooling the shadows: On the Blue curve add (0.25, 0.3); on the Red curve add (0.25, 0.22). Shadows shift toward blue while the highlights stay neutral.
- Fixing a specific tone: Use Pick a point on a face, then drag that point up or down a few percent; only tones near it move.
### FAQ
Q: How many points can a curve have?
A: Between 2 and 16 per curve, with the x values strictly increasing. The two end points can be moved vertically but not removed; any point in between can be dragged or deleted.
Q: Why does the curve never overshoot between points?
A: It is a Fritsch-Carlson monotone cubic: slopes at each point are limited so a segment between two points stays between their y values. A steep rise still reaches its top point exactly but cannot bulge past it the way a free cubic spline would.
Q: Which curve is applied first, RGB or the color channels?
A: Red, Green and Blue first, each on its own channel, then the RGB curve on all three outputs. So an RGB S-curve adds contrast to the already color-corrected channels.
Q: How precise is the 256-entry table?
A: Each table entry is a float sampled at i / 255, and a pixel value between two entries is linearly interpolated, so the error against the exact spline is far below one 8-bit level for any smooth curve.
Q: What does the eyedropper do?
A: Pick a point from the photo adds a point to the current curve at the x position of the value under the cursor (the luma for RGB, or that channel's value), with y equal to x so nothing changes until you drag it.
Q: Can curves fix a color cast?
A: Yes. Find a neutral gray with the eyedropper on each channel and drag the resulting points until the three outputs agree, or raise the input end of the deficient channel. For casts from lighting, white balance is usually faster.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when someone wants precise tone or colour shaping with a draggable curve for RGB and each channel, up to 16 points, such as an S-curve for contrast or a faded matte look.
When to send them elsewhere: For just black and white points use Levels (photo-levels); for a single contrast change use Adjust contrast (adjust-image-contrast); exposure problems belong in Fix exposure (fix-photo-exposure). If the grade is a .cube file use Apply a LUT (apply-lut-to-photo).
